title: Jesus’ rebuke of Peter. Part 3
scripture_text: ‘’From that time on Jesus began to explain to his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, the chief priests and the teachers of the law, and that he must be killed and on the third day be raised to life. Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. “Never, Lord!” he said. “This shall never happen to you!”
devotional:
Jesus turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me; you do not have in mind the concerns of God, but merely human concerns.” Then Jesus said to his disciples, “Whoever wants to be my disciple, must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me will find it. What good will it be for someone to gain the whole world, yet forfeit their soul? Or what can anyone give in exchange for their soul? For the Son of Man is going to come in his Father’s glory with his angels, and then he will reward each person according to what they have done.’’

Before we look at what Jesus meant when he said 'Take up your cross and follow me,' we need to make a few observations that will help us in our understanding. Depending on what version of the bible you read, the phrase 'take up your cross' is either found five or six times. Many of the older translations include the phrase in Mark 10:21 as part of Jesus’ response to the Rich Young Ruler, while the more modern translations don't. If you look carefully at every context in which Jesus uses the phrase, it is also in the context of difficult relationships.

In Matthew 10:34-37 Jesus is speaking about difficult relationships, and how the demands of the Kingdom can put great strain on family relationships then He says in Matthew 10:38 'And anyone who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.' This is similar to the context in Luke 14:27 'And whosoever does not carry his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple.' The main difference being, that in Matthew 10 Jesus was speaking to the twelve, while in Luke 14 He is speaking to the crowds.

The references in Matthew 16:24, Mark 8:34 and Luke 9:23 are all in the context of Peter's confession and rebuke of Jesus, although Luke does not mention that Peter rebuked Jesus. However this was a time of personal tension between the two. If we include Mark 10:21, that too, was also in the context of a strained relationship between the Rich Young Ruler and Jesus. When we think of Jesus taking up his own cross, that was to mend broken relationships between God and man, so as we try to understand what 'taking up your cross’ really means, we need to keep in mind the contexts in which Jesus spoke this command.

A second thing we need to keep in mind is that we must not turn the cross that Jesus was speaking of here into something it isn't. Many people think that a cross is any trial or hardship they are going through, such as, a health problem, a disability, bereavement, or being single. 'That's my cross,' we say, but this is not what Jesus meant. The problem with this understanding is that most of the pain we go through in life is not of our own choosing. I didn't waken up one morning and think Cerebral Palsy is the cross for me, so l chose my disability. No! When it comes to most of the trials and difficulties in life, we don't have a choice, but when it comes to taking up our cross we do have a choice.

When we read these verses about taking up your cross, we must remember that the context in which Matthew 16 places this teaching, is intended to refute the influence and mindset of Satan. What Jesus is going to teach about taking up you cross is designed to protect us from Satanic influence.

So what is Jesus referring to when He speaks about our cross?

Crucifixion in the Ancient World.

The cross in Jesus' day was an instrument of torture and execution, pure and simple. There wasn't a figurative use of 'cross' as a 'burden' or 'trial' in those days. Death on the cross was a shameful, excruciating, way to die. An ancient Greek poem describes it this way: Punished with limbs outstretched, they see the stake as their fate; They are fastened (and) nailed to it in the most bitter torment, evil food for birds of prey and grim pickings for dogs.'

Psuedo-Manetho, Apotelesmatica 4:198ff, cited by Martin Hengel, Crucifixion (Fortress Press, translated 1977), p. 9.

'At that time these words of Jesus might have been rendered thus: 'If anyone wishes to come after me, let him be prepared to be led out to public execution, following my example' (The Hard Sayings of Jesus, F. F. Bruce, p. 150).

There was no 'norm' for execution on the cross, though it often included flogging beforehand, the victim carrying the beam to the place of execution, being nailed to it with outstretched arms, raised up, and seated on a small wooden peg. But Seneca indicates there were many variations: 'I see crosses there, not just of one kind but made in many different ways: some have their victims with head down to the ground; some impale their private parts; others stretch out their arms on the gibbet. "[15] Seneca, Dialogue 6 (De consolatione ad Marciam) 20.3. Cited by Hengel, p. 25

Josephus, an eyewitness of Roman cruelty to the defenders at the fall of Jerusalem in 70 AD, gives us a gruesome picture:

‘They were first whipped, and then tormented with all sorts of tortures, before they died, and were then crucified before the wall of the city. This miserable procedure made Titus greatly to pity them, while they caught every day five hundred Jews; nay, some days they caught more.' The main reason why he did not forbid that cruelty was that he hoped the Jews might perhaps yield at that sight, out of fear lest they might themselves afterwards be liable to the same cruel treatment. So the soldiers, out of the wrath and hatred they bore the Jews, nailed those they caught, one after one, and another after another, to the crosses, by way of jest, when their multitude was so great, that room was wanting for the crosses, and crosses wanting for the bodies.' Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 5, 11.

After a revolt following the death of Herod the Great, the Roman proconsul Varus crucified two thousand Jews. Crucifixion was a common practice in the Roman Empire.

When Jesus said, 'Take up your cross,' the disciples saw poor condemned souls marching along a road with the instrument of their own death strapped to their backs. Carrying one's cross meant walking to one's death.

Is Jesus not being a bit extreme?

What is the point of being crucified? Surely God has come to give us life to the full! So why would we want to carry a cross? And what is our cross anyway?

The cross that Jesus is speaking about may not lead to physical death, in fact there may not be anything physical to it. What Jesus is referring to is the heart attitude of a cross bearer.

Or to put it in the form of a question: -

What kind of heart attitudes did Jesus display as he carried His cross?

Jesus was expressing an attitude of love, forgiveness, humility and submission as he bowed to, and suffered in the will of God. The attitudes and motives Jesus needed to die on the cross, are the same attitudes and motives we need for life.
prayer: Father I need to recognise that the cross I need to carry is an essential for my spiritual well-being.
